> 📍 **階層**: Home > News > UK
![Sad woman in dark room. Depression concept.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_313737178-c403.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646)
A new report from Refuge, the UK’s largest domestic abuse charity, and the End Violence Against Women Coalition reveals 36% of women experienced some form of violence online (Picture: Getty Images)
**[Social media](https://metro.co.uk/tag/social-media/) algorithms are ‘normalising’ violence against women and girls, with one in three subjected to ‘shocking levels of abuse’ every day.**

A new report from Refuge, the UK’s largest domestic abuse [charity](https://metro.co.uk/tag/charity/), and the End Violence Against Women Coalition reveals 36% of women experienced some form of violence online.
That number rises to 47% for women aged between 16 and 24.
A fifth of those said they encountered the same misogynistic content pumped into the manosphere ‘to maximise ad revenue’ most of or every time they logged on.
The online harms are having significant real-world consequences, with victims suffering [anxiety](https://metro.co.uk/tag/anxiety/) or panic attacks and being driven from the platforms completely.
Most worryingly, 7% of women who experienced online violence said they felt suicidal – a figure which more than doubles (15%) among those aged 16 to 24.
Refuge CEO Gemma Sherrington said their findings ‘are reflective of a system that has continued to prioritise profits over safety, leaving women to pay the price’.
## **Jodie’s story**
In January 2021, Jodie\* opened an anonymous email directing her to images of herself which had been shared online, along with details identifying her and where she lived.
Weeks later she discovered explicit ‘deepfakes’ of her on an online forum.
Her ‘shock and desperation’ turned to ‘complete fear, anger and disbelief’ when she found out the perpetrator was her male best friend.
Jodie successfully campaigned with EVAW for the creation of non-consensual sexually explicit deepfakes to become a crime (Picture: EVAW)

Among the women polled by Refuge and EVAW, one in 50 reported they had personally experienced an AI-generated or ‘[deepfake](https://metro.co.uk/tag/deepfake/)’ intimate image of them being shared without their consent.
Nearly three quarters (72%) identified the perpetrator as male, with current or former partners and friends or relatives each responsible in roughly a fifth of cases.
The most commonly identified perpetrator (53%) was a stranger.
When Jodie went to the police to report the abuse, she was told there was ‘nothing they could do’.
She had to track down the images and videos herself, contacting the online forum and porn site directly to get the material taken down.
‘Gathering the evidence was incredibly distressing and retraumatising. It felt as though the responsibility for proving the harm had been placed entirely on me,’ she told Metro.
After going through that process and collecting the evidence, Jodie was told the creation and sharing of sexually explicit deepfakes had not broken any laws, so her abuser could not be prosecuted.

‘Despite the threats and risks I was facing, I did not have a liaison officer, and was told I was unable to access an Independent Sexual Violence Adviser because the abuse was not considered sexually motivated,’ Jodie said.
‘Survivors should not have to repeatedly explain, document and prove their abuse while navigating systems that do not understand the nature of online harms.
‘Evidence gathering and reporting need to be trauma-informed, coordinated and designed around the safety of the person experiencing the abuse.
‘The burden should not fall on survivors to become experts in criminal investigations, technology and platform reporting while they are trying to recover.’

Far-right activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested after he was filmed slashing the side of a dinghy in the English Channel with a rescue crew member still on board.

The 37-year-old, also known as Danny Tommo, uploaded footage on YouTube appearing to show him being arrested, with the officer telling him he is being detained on suspicion of criminal damage “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.
In earlier footage on YouTube, he appeared to shout “traitors” and use a knife to cut the side of the vessel that had been used by people smugglers to transport migrants in the Channel.

![A large group of people standing on a road, some wearing English and British flags](//image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/bf4081aa275036408e3eb4f190f5347dY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzkwMTk0Mzg1/2.85938900.jpg?w=640)
Police and protesters in Gosport, Hampshire (Trevor Adams/PA)
He could be seen slashing and stabbing the small boat after a member of a rescue crew had boarded to apparently take the vessel back to France.
Mr Thomas appears to have also filmed his own arrest following the incident in a video streamed on his channel last night.
The footage shows Mr Thomas getting out of a car which looked to be blocked in by other vehicles at a petrol station.
He can be heard asking police if he can use his phone to speak to his children.
One officer is recorded saying: “The information that I’ve been given… is that you’ve been involved in criminal damage recklessly endangering someone’s life.”
Mr Thomas then repeatedly said: “I understand.”
A boat containing 51 migrants who refused help from the French coastguard and spent more than 30 hours at sea has arrived in Dover.
A Hampshire Police statement said: “A man has been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder on board, was damaged in the English Channel.
“We received a report of the incident on Tuesday evening.

“Last night, a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, was arrested on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety under Section 11 of the Aviation and Maritime Security Act 1990, criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals under Section 58 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1995.
“He remains in custody at this time.”
Hundreds of activists gathered in Gosport on Tuesday after Mr Thomas filmed himself going out to sea to try to intercept a dinghy carrying dozens of migrants.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said three people have been charged after they gathered at the marina where they thought the boat’s passengers were due to arrive.
![A man in handcuffs is led away by police](//image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/194571fb4a8d66ae513079ade6c8924eY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzkwMjQ0MTA2/2.85940572.jpg?w=640)
A person is led away by police during a protest in Gosport (Trevor Adams/PA)
Six people were arrested by officers during the evening, the force said.
Shannon Dodds, 32, of Gosport, has been charged with two counts of assault by beating of an emergency worker. She has been remanded in custody to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates Court on Thursday.

Sally Pearson, 31, also of Gosport, has been charged with assault by beating of an emergency worker and a racially aggravated public order offence. She has also been remanded in custody to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates Court on Thursday.
Toby Matthews, 33, from Gosport, has been charged with common assault of an emergency worker. He was bailed to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates Court on November 9.
Some of the protesters in Gosport wore black clothing and face coverings, and chanted “send them back”, wrongly assuming the boat would be guided to the Hampshire coast.
In fact, it docked in Dover, Kent, at around 12.30am on Wednesday after 51 migrants on board reportedly refused help from a French ship and spent 33 hours at sea.

The University of Stirling has opened registration for the first event in the 2026 ESRC Festival of Social Science programme.
A hybrid event, ‘Adapting Housing for a Changing Future’ will take place on 4 November 2026, 2.00pm to 4.00pm at the University of Stirling Campus Central and online.

The summer of 2026 has highlighted how changing weather patterns are affecting our homes and communities. At the same time, Scotland faces other major challenges, including an ageing population and the need to ensure homes remain accessible and suitable throughout people’s lives.

While housing debates often focus on new developments, much of the challenge lies in adapting existing homes. This event will explore what social science research can tell us about creating housing that is resilient, accessible and fit for the future.
Attendees will hear from:

-   Professor Vikki McCall (Housing and Social Policy)
-   Dr Vanicka Arora (Heritage Studies)
-   Professor Lesley Palmer (Ageing and Dementia Design)
This hybrid event is aimed at housing professionals, policymakers, practitioners and anyone with an interest in the future of housing.

Five vacant flats in Portree are set to be refurbished and brought back into use through a partnership between SSEN Transmission and Lochalsh and Skye Housing Association (LSHA).

The properties, located within the Leathad na Sobhraig development, will undergo a comprehensive refurbishment programme before being designated as accommodation for key staff supporting the delivery of SSEN Transmission’s Skye Reinforcement Project.

As part of the initiative, wider improvements will also be carried out to the North and South blocks at Leathad na Sobhraig. The programme includes repairs and upgrades to the external building and common areas, including the removal of cladding, structural enhancements, and guttering work. A full internal fit-out will also be completed as part of the upgrades to the five flats.

Initially, the refurbished homes will be used to accommodate staff working on the SSEN Transmission Skye Reinforcement Project – a major electricity transmission project which involves replacing the existing electricity infrastructure between Fort Augustus and Ardmore in Skye.
This temporary use of the flats ensures the properties are put to immediate and practical use, supporting local economic activities.
Once work on the Skye Reinforcement Project is complete, SSEN Transmission will return all five upgraded homes to LSHA for allocation to local tenants.

The refurbishment works will be fully funded through the partnership between SSEN Transmission and LSHA. The initiative has also been supported by the Scottish Government, which reviewed and approved the mechanism enabling the refurbishment and improvement works to proceed.

LSHA are engaging with local contractors to complete the projects. The refurbishment works will be delivered by Torr Civils & Building LTD, a contractor based in Raasay with experience across building, renovation and refurbishment projects throughout Skye and the Highlands.
Works are expected to begin in the coming weeks and are anticipated to take around four months to complete.

Chris Bell, project director at SSEN Transmission, said: “The Skye Reinforcement Project will support local employment and bring workers to the island during construction. “We’re pleased to support a project that not only helps us deliver the infrastructure needed for Skye’s future but also leaves a positive legacy for the local community.”

Lowri Richards, LSHA chief executive, said: “The purchase and refurbishment of the five flats is an important step in supporting the long-term occupation and management of the entire Leathad na Sobhraig development.

Architecture appears to be at a permanent crossroads: a profession in a state of perpetual crisis and reappraisal. The problems that have plagued the profession in recent years – low fees, mounting workloads, increased liability, diminishing autonomy and the gradual erosion of the architect’s role – are being compounded by rapid technological change and an increasingly uncertain global economy.
For students entering the profession, the question is becoming increasingly stark: what, exactly, are they being educated for?

The pressures facing young people entering the workforce aren’t unique to architecture. Earlier this year, the government announced that the number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training (NEETs) had reached a staggering one million. [And architecture offers little immunity](https://www.architectsjournal.co.uk/news/into-work-the-crisis-in-architecture-early-careers). One recent indication of the competition for entry-level positions came from JTP, [which received 2,600 applications](https://www.architectsjournal.co.uk/news/opinion/a-plea-to-architecture-practices-keep-employing-part-1s) for just nine Part 1 architectural assistant roles.

At the same time, architectural education itself is changing. The [ARB’s reforms](https://www.architectsjournal.co.uk/news/arb-scraps-2-year-requirement-in-professional-practical-experience-shake-up) are prompting universities to rethink how courses are structured. Some institutions are moving towards integrated qualifications, others are withdrawing degree offerings, and some architecture departments are closing altogether. Apprenticeship routes are changing, too.

Against this backdrop, the debate about the future of the profession has increasingly turned towards questions of numbers. If there are not enough jobs for architecture graduates, should fewer people be studying it in the first place? But before we ask this, perhaps we should ask a more fundamental question: what is an architecture degree for?

The answer is, perhaps, less straightforward than it once was. An architectural education has always been more than simply preparing someone to draw buildings. It teaches students to interrogate complex problems, communicate ideas, work collaboratively, navigate constraints and think critically, technically and spatially. It demands research, synthesis, iteration and the ability to make decisions in conditions of uncertainty.
> The much-vaunted ‘transferable skills’ of an architecture degree are rarely discussed in concrete terms

These skills have obvious value far beyond the traditional boundaries of architectural practice, but the much-vaunted ‘transferable skills’ of an architecture degree are rarely discussed in concrete terms. Where exactly can they be applied?

What usually functions as a response is the examples of architecture graduates who move into planning, property, film, journalism, exhibition design or other sectors; evidence that their degree has at least equipped them to do something else.

However, the breadth of architectural education is not just a useful by-product of training to become an architect. It is one of its defining characteristics. The ability to understand competing interests, work across scales, translate between different forms of knowledge and turn abstract ideas into something tangible has value whether or not the result is a building.

This year’s [AJ Student Prize](https://www.architectsjournal.co.uk/practice/students/aj-student-prize) reveals that breadth. A new £5 million fund will help communities improve preparedness and reduce flood risk.
Opening in 2027, the £5m Community Flood Resilience Fund is a key element of the additional £15m investment in flood prevention set out in the recent Programme for Government (PfG).
The fund will allocate £1m directly to community applications and £4m to local authorities applying with communities to deliver local flood resilience measures.
This investment will empower local people and organisations to play a leading role in reducing flood risk and improving preparedness in their communities for any future flooding events.

A further £2.5m from the £15m total announced in the PfG will be available to local authorities to future-proof public assets and resilience infrastructure, making the most of the flood protection already in place. Another £3m will target local authority projects that use nature to support flooding solutions, such as managing rainfall and water-flow through planting design.
Innovative coastal projects to replenish sand dunes and reduce flood risk will receive up to £1m, and £500,000 will be made available to help communities recovering from recent flooding.

Details of the funding are set out in the [Flood Resilience Strategy Implementation Plan](https://www.gov.scot/publications/national-flood-resilience-strategy-implementation-plan/), outlining 65 actions organisations across Scotland will take over the next four years to improve Scotland’s flood resilience. The [Implementation of the Flood Risk Management Act Report 2021 -2025](https://www.gov.scot/publications/national-flood-resilience-strategy-implementation-report-2021-2025/) is also published and sets out the steps taken since 2021.

Climate action and rural affairs secretary Gillian Martin said: “Flood resilience is about more than managing water. It is about how we plan our towns and cities, protect vital infrastructure, manage land, and support our communities to adapt. From strategy to the implementation plan published today, we are setting out how we will protect people and places across the country from the increased flood risk as a result of climate change over the next four years.

“Since 2016, the Scottish Government has invested £612m to support local authority flood risk management, helping to deliver 21 flood protection schemes, with four further projects under construction, two under contract, and three progressing through development.

“In addition to these significant investments we have a strong track record on working with nature to strengthen our resilience to a changing climate through restoring our rivers and peatlands, planting more trees and wider nature-based solutions. On the heels of [London Design Festival](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/london-design-festival/), we have [rounded up](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/roundups/) a selection of furniture and products presented during the city-wide event made of scraps that would otherwise have gone to waste.

[London Design Festival](https://londondesignfestival.com/) (LDF) concluded on Sunday, after a week of product launches, exhibitions and installations that showed the best of the capital's design scene.

Throughout the event, a trend that stood out was the presence of designers using materials leftover from manufacturing, whether as an attempt to slash costs, preserve resources or simply experiment visually.
Here are seven examples of the technique spotted during London's main design week:
![Dagwood Bench](https://static.dezeen.com/uploads/2026/09/dagwood-bench-852x852.jpg)
Top: photo by Lewis Duckworth. Above: photo by Carmel King
**Dagwood Bench by Lewis Duckworth**

[Lewis Duckworth](https://www.instagram.com/lewis_duck_duck_goose/) is one of London's many emerging talents. As the co-founder of guerrilla collective [Design Everything](http://dezeen.com/tag/design-everything), he is always looking for ways to create furniture with the [inevitable limitations](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/09/22/with-limitations-aram-design-everything/) that come with being a young, independent designer.
Dagwood Bench is one such project, made from timber end pieces leftover from furniture production, which are often too narrow or short to be reused and would normally go to waste.

Duckworth created the bench from a single laminated plank, sandwiched between two timber faces. The designer explained that offcuts were arranged within these pieces of wood to create a form that "appears visually thick while remaining lightweight and structurally capable".

"This project explores ways to re-evaluate these 'un-usable' elements by incorporating them into a larger, cohesive material system," he said. "Given that they started as an industrial byproduct, it felt most appropriate to reprocess them in a standardised format".

Duckworth's Dagwood Bench is among the 34-strong shortlist of buildings, furniture and objects nominated for a 2026 [Wood Award](https://www.woodawards.com/). A selection of these designs were on display at the [Material Matters](https://www.dezeen.com/eventsguide/2026/09/material-matters-ldf-2026/) exhibition during LDF.
![Spared](https://static.dezeen.com/uploads/2026/09/spared-material-offcuts-birds-852x852.jpg)
**Second Song by Spared**
Second Song is a selection of bird-shaped collectible objects by Brighton-based design studio [Spared](https://spared.eco/).

The studio is known for transforming waste generated from its own varied practice into furniture and products, such as [tables made from old coffee grounds](https://www.dezeen.com/2023/08/04/tate-modern-corner-cafe-holland-harvey/) developed for the Corner cafe at London's Tate Modern museum.

Cast using a resin-free mineral binder, the collectible birds were made of offcuts ranging from shell and stone to workshop sawdust and thin scrapings from the surfaces of plastic chopping boards used in industrial kitchens.
Second Song was another project presented at Material Matters.
